    Canadian rock singer Sass Jordan, voice behind ‘Make You a Believer’ and ‘Tell Somebody,’ dies at 63

    SECTIONS
    Canadian rock singer Sass Jordan, voice behind ‘Make You a Believer’ and ‘Tell Somebody,’ dies at 63
    By
    Rana Sarkar
    , Global DeskLast Updated: Oct 04, 2026, 08:25:00 AM IST
    Synopsis

    Sass Jordan, the renowned Canadian rock singer, has passed away at the age of 63. Her family reported that she died peacefully, surrounded by loved ones. Jordan had faced health issues recently, which led to the cancellation of her performances. Born in Birmingham and raised in Montreal, she became a prominent figure in the music industry.

    Canadian rock singer Sass Jordan, who was behind ‘Racine’ and ‘Make You a Believer,’ has died at 63. Her family says she passed away peacefully, surrounded by loved ones. According to a statement posted on her social media account, Jordan ‘crossed over to the other side’ on Saturday, October 2, 2026. The post described the Montreal-raised singer as an “inimitable force of nature” and an “irreplaceable being of light and joy.”


    Sass Jordan’s cause of death is unknown; past illness caused show’s cancellation


    Sass Jordan’s cause of death is not known, but she recently had some health issues that led to the cancellation of her show. Last month, her representatives announced the cancellation in a media release, stating that she had been advised to step away from all engagements for the rest of 2026.

    “Unfortunately, due to a serious medical condition, Sass is currently unable to perform and has been advised to step away from all professional commitments for the remainder of 2026 to focus on her health and recovery,” the statement read, as quoted by Fort Frances Times on September 1.

    “As a result, we regret that we need to cancel her remaining scheduled performances for this year. Sass is very sorry for the inconvenience and disappointment this may cause and greatly appreciates your understanding under these circumstances. Thank you for your patience and consideration,” it adds. She was scheduled to perform on September 16. However, the exact nature of Jordan’s illness was not disclosed.

    Live Events


        Who was Sarah Jordon?


        Born Sarah Jordan in Birmingham, England, in 1962, Jordan moved to Montreal with her family when she was three. She later became one of Canada's best-known female rock singers.

        Her music career began gaining attention in the late 1980s. Her debut album, Tell Somebody, was released in 1988, with its title track reaching #11 in Canada. It produced several Canadian hits and earned her a Juno Award for Most Promising Female Vocalist the next year.

        Jordan reached a new level of success with her 1992 album Racine. The record included some of her most recognized songs, such as Make You a Believer, I Want to Believe, You Don’t Have to Remind Me and Goin’ Back Again.

        Make You a Believer also reached the Billboard Mainstream Rock chart. Billboard named Jordan its top female rock artist of 1992, cementing her place among Canada's leading rock performers.

        AI was everywhere at GFF 2026. Full automation was not

        SECTIONS
        AI was everywhere at GFF 2026. Full automation was not
        By
        Gaurab Dasgupta
        &
        Arun Padmanabhan
        , ET Spotlight SpecialLast Updated: Oct 18, 2026, 09:04:00 PM IST
        Rate Story

        Synopsis

        Global Fintech Fest 2026 highlighted agentic AI's practical integration within the BFSI sector. Automation will handle basic tasks, but humans will retain final decision-making authority. Companies are focusing on specialised AI models and optimizing compute power for cost efficiency. Job roles are evolving, with a continued emphasis on hiring and upskilling employees.

        The Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 concluded in Mumbai on September 11, bringing together financial institutions, fintech companies, regulators and technology providers from more than 70 countries. In keeping with this year’s theme, agentic AI dominated conversations on and off the stage.

        YuVerse launches four last-mile AI products | GFF 2026

        At Global Fintech Fest 2026, YuVerse CEO and Co-founder Mathangi Sri Ramachandran spoke to The Economic Times about the company’s last-mile AI proposition and its four product launches across credit decisioning, conversational AI, video creation and workflow automation.
        By the time the conference ended, the conversation had spilled beyond the venue. At a post-event mixer, a restaurant ticker screen flashed: “yekya AI AI laga rakha hai”. It was a joke, but it captured the mood. AI was everywhere.


        Beyond the buzz, however, conversations with founders and senior executives across the tightly regulated banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) sector were increasingly practical. The debate was less about whether AI would be used and more about where an agent should stop, which model fits a task, and what adoption means beyond applications and data centres.

        From AI Pilots to Business Impact: Redesigning Work for the AI Era

        AI is moving beyond pilots and productivity tools as businesses rethink how work gets done, where AI creates value, and where human judgement remains essential.At the Accenture B-School Challenge, leaders from BMW Group India, SBI Cards, Ashoka University, Levi’s GCC, Nestlé, and Accenture share perspectives on AI adoption, ROI, workforce readiness, and responsible scaling. From redesigning workflows to building trusted data foundations, the discussion explores what it will take to turn AI from a tool into a business capability.Watch the full panel discussion to understand how organisations are preparing for the next phase of AI-led business transformation.

        100% automation not on the cards

        Live Events


            ‘Humans are not going out of the loop’ was one of the biggest takeaways from GFF 2026. Several discussions prompted the question of whether agentic AI will facilitate end-to-end transactions and decision-making. According to Perfios Group CEO Nitin Chugh, the answer is no. Parts of the workflow, such as low-level basic tasks (code generation) that are repetitive, could get automated, but humans will always make the final call.


            Building Wealth With Fractional Real Estate | FabInvest | The Economic Times

            In this episode of the ET Podcast, Dr. Ravi Teja, Founder and CEO of FabInvest, discusses how fractional ownership is changing the way investors access real estate in India. He discusses how this system of ownership is making high-value real estate more accessible to small- and mid-scale investors, and is bringing in investment opportunities in premium properties at discounts of up to 30–35% off market prices.

            However, the role of an underwriter will change. Earlier, if they could process 10 loan applications, AI can enable them to process significantly more applications, Chugh suggested.


            Also Read: BFSI sector in no hurry to adopt complete automation: Perfios Group CEO

            Meanwhile, HyperVerge’s business-loan underwriting suite shows what that division of work can look like. Its agents pull information from bank statements, goods and services tax filings and income-tax returns, flag gaps, run background checks and assemble credit notes.

            Empowering MSMEs: MIDC’s Vision for Inclusive Growth in Maharashtra | Deependra Singh Kushwah | MIDC | Economic Times

            Deependra Singh Kushwah, IAS, CEO of Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation (MIDC), shares how the state is empowering over 10 million MSMEs to drive its next phase of industrial growth. He highlighted key MIDC initiatives, from reserving 20% land in industrial parks for MSMEs and setting up common facility centers to easing access to credit, technology, and global markets. Discover how local enterprises are integrating into high-tech sectors like semiconductors and advanced manufacturing to build a stronger supply chain.

            “Today, a credit underwriter examines bank statements, GST filings and income-tax returns, and then prepares a note for the team. If preparing that note takes two hours, AI can create it in about a minute,” HyperVerge cofounder and CEO Kedar Kulkarni said. The lending decision, however, remains with the credit manager.


            The industry is also increasingly aware that compute power is not free. It is

            imperative to understand which tasks need to be automated and which can be done manually to save both time and money. Companies such as KFintech, Zeta, and Perfios are adopting this route by only adopting agentic workflows in processes where absolutely mandatory, to minimise their AI spend as well.


            Jobs change, but hiring continues

            ‘Will AI take our jobs?’ is another question that you will find as a part of every conversation on the subject. At GFF, the answer was fairly and surprisingly optimistic.

            Revolut India’s CEO Paroma Chatterjee said ‘making people redundant due to AI is a no-win’. The company plans to hire about 1,500 people in India in 2026. She said it is critical to create AI-targeted jobs and build workflows that have AI embedded in the design thinking.


            However, roles built around repetitive tasks are likely to see the biggest disruption, while employees in more senior positions will increasingly be expected to handle higher-value work rather than routine processing.

            Zeta's APAC CEO Ramki Gaddipati told us that the firm's coding teams have moved away from basic code-writing towards reviewing AI-generated code, with AI agents handling the first level of coding.



            Smaller, specialised models find their moment

            For financial companies operating under strict regulatory and data-security requirements, the attraction of AI is increasingly about using the right model for the right job rather than simply deploying the biggest available large language model (LLM).

            This is creating interest in smaller, specialised and domain-specific models that can be deployed for particular use cases, while giving companies greater control over sensitive data and costs.

            For instance, KFintech, the country’s largest Registrar and Transfer Agent (RTA), has used open-weight models from Alibaba’s Qwen to build a more specialised AI system for its operations. Since the company deals with large volumes of sensitive data, it believes that having its own SLM is more beneficial.


            Mastercard's AI Garage, meanwhile, has built a large tabular model (LTM) for transaction data, allowing the company to work with characteristics specific to its payments data.

            Revolut India has also developed PRAGMA, a family of transformer-based models designed to analyse customers' financial histories as temporal signals, using NVIDIA's Llama-Nemotron-Embed-1B-v2.


            Voice AI finds its way into finance

            Voice AI was another prominent theme at GFF, but the conversation had moved beyond scripted sales calls. Companies are increasingly looking at voice as an interface through which customers can ask questions, buy financial products, and seek assistance without navigating complex applications.

            One example came from ONDC. The network’s chief business officer for financial services, Hrushikesh Mehta, said a network participant is testing a voice assistant that helps autorickshaw drivers in Bengaluru invest as little as Rs 20 in mutual funds.

            Arrowhead AI cofounder and CEO Devyani Gupta described contextual voice agents being used in lending, while Policybazaar CTO Bibhu Krishna said the insurance platform is using voice systems for outbound calls and piloting an open-ended inbound bot for motor insurance.


            Also Read: Voice AI startup Arrowhead eyes fresh funding to accelerate international expansion

            The interface could lower the cost of reaching customers, especially in smaller towns and across local languages.

            But the technology also brings a new set of risks. If AI can convincingly recreate a person’s voice, voice-based verification becomes less reliable.

            Krishna pointed to attempts involving proxy voices and images during life-insurance video KYC. He also said fully autonomous policy issuance is not yet on the table, with people still needed for nuanced questions, including those involving claims ratios. Voice may become the entry point to a financial workflow, but identity checks and complex decisions will still need human escalation.

            Adoption is high. Depth is another question

            BCG’s flagship GFF 2026 report, Balance: Thriving in the Age of AI, points to India’s high workplace adoption. BCG’s AI at Work 2026 survey found that 70% of Indian frontline AI users said the tools saved them at least one full workday a week, the highest share among the markets covered, while 96% said AI had changed the skills required in their roles.

            But widespread use does not necessarily mean India is building capabilities across the technology stack.

            Also Read: India’s banks could turn legacy tech into an AI advantage: BCG

            Conversations with fintech executives at GFF suggested that much of the adoption is happening either at the application layer, where companies are racing to build workflows and services on established models, or at the infrastructure layer, where billions of dollars are being committed to data centres and computing capacity.

            This raises two problems: India has a relatively small number of companies building India-focused foundation models, including Sarvam and BharatGen, while the country's semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem is still developing.

            For the BFSI sector, however, the immediate AI opportunity may not depend on India building a frontier model of its own. The more immediate question is how effectively financial companies can use existing models, while keeping data secure, controlling costs, and retaining human oversight over the decisions that matter.

            The ₹1 Crore Portfolio Problem: When Your Money Grows, Your Mistakes Get More Expensive

            SECTIONS
            The ₹1 Crore Portfolio Problem: When Your Money Grows, Your Mistakes Get More Expensive
            ET SpotlightLast Updated: Oct 13, 2026, 10:28:00 AM IST
            Rate Story
            Follow us
            Share
            Font Size
            AbcSmall
            AbcMedium
            AbcLarge
            Save
            Print
            Comment
            Synopsis

            Market corrections can influence portfolios differently depending on their size and the investor's timeline. Investors with larger portfolios need a careful approach to risk management amid market fluctuations. Those with long-term aspirations should keep funds for short-term needs separate from their growth capital. This tactic guarantees that financial commitments are fulfilled even during market downturns.

            Listen to this article in summarized format

            A market correction is expressed in percentages. Investors experience it in rupees.

            A 10% fall on a ₹10 lakh portfolio means ₹1 lakh. On ₹50 lakh, it is ₹5 lakh. At ₹1 crore, the same correction translates into ₹10 lakh.

            Nothing has changed in percentage terms. Everything changes in terms of numbers. A Rs. 10 lakh fall in portfolio value has a higher psychological impact compared to Rs. 1 lakh, even when the percentage drop is the same.

            Bonds Corner

Rising crude oil prices and a hawkish central bank stance have impacted the market negatively. The benchmark repo rate was recently raised to 5.5%, with further increases expected. The 2036 bond yield rose to 7.4740%, indicating a broader trend of increasing yields. These developments may significantly affect India's import bill and inflation outlook.

            Browse all Bonds News with

            That is why asset allocation becomes increasingly important as the portfolio grows. The objective is not necessarily to take less risk. It is to decide which part of the money can remain exposed to market cycles, and which part already has a financial obligation attached to it.

            September 2026 offered a timely reminder.

            Live Events


                The Same Correction, a Very Different Experience

                The Nifty 50 had one of its toughest months in years in September, with the September series falling nearly 7%. The index is now roughly 14% below its all-time high.

                But the current phase is not just a price correction.

                Indian equities have also spent close to two years struggling to make meaningful progress. Investors have effectively experienced a time correction alongside a price correction.

                For long-term equity investors, neither is unusual. The problem begins when money that may be required in the next few years is sitting in the same portfolio as money intended for retirement 15 years later.

                Consider what a 10% correction means at different corpus levels:

                Portfolio sizeLoss after a 10% correction
                ₹10 lakh₹1 lakh
                ₹50 lakh₹5 lakh
                ₹1 crore₹10 lakh
                At ₹10 lakh, an investor in the accumulation phase may be able to continue investing and wait for recovery.

                At ₹1 crore, a ₹10 lakh decline could represent a year's college fees, a home down payment or several years of planned family expenses.

                The larger the corpus becomes, the more expensive poor allocation decisions become.

                ₹1 Crore Needs More Than One Time Horizon

                A ₹1 crore portfolio is rarely meant for a single goal.

                Some of it may be retirement money that can remain invested for another decade or more. Another portion may be required for children's education, a home purchase, parents' medical expenses, or other commitments over the next three to five years.

                These two pools should not necessarily carry the same market risk.

                If the entire ₹1 crore remains exposed to equities and the market corrects 15%, the portfolio falls to ₹85 lakh.

                That decline itself may be temporary. The bigger risk is being forced to withdraw money while the portfolio is still recovering. This is where allocation becomes less about predicting markets and more about creating financial flexibility.

                What ₹30 Lakh in Bonds Changes

                Consider dividing the ₹1 crore portfolio into:

                ₹70 lakh in equities

                ₹30 lakh in bonds

                If equities fall 15%, the equity allocation declines by ₹10.5 lakh to ₹59.5 lakh.

                Assuming, purely for illustration, that the bond portfolio remains unchanged, the overall portfolio would stand at ₹89.5 lakh.

                The total declineis 10.5%, not 15%.

                Portfolio structureValue after 15% equity correctionDecline
                ₹1 crore in equities₹85 lakh₹15 lakh
                ₹70 lakh equity + ₹30 lakh bonds*₹89.5 lakh₹10.5 lakh
                The bond allocation reduces the immediate portfolio impact by ₹4.5 lakh. But that is only one part of its role.

                When Equities Need Time, Bonds Can Provide Cash Flow

                A time correction changes the portfolio equation because investors may have to wait longer for equity returns to materialize.

                The fixed-income portion can continue doing a different job during that period.

                If the ₹30 lakh bond portfolio earns an illustrative average yield of 10%, it could generate around ₹3 lakh in annual interest before tax, depending on individual coupon structures.

                That cash flow can be mapped to upcoming expenses rather than requiring an investor to sell equities during a weak market.

                This is a more useful way to think about bonds in a large portfolio. They are not there because equities have fallen or because investors should suddenly become conservative. They are there because not every rupee has the same time horizon.

                Online bond platforms such as Jiraaf can help investors evaluate listed corporate bonds across credit ratings, maturities, yields, and payout frequencies. This lets you build the fixed-income allocation around when you may need the money, rather than treating debt as a generic percentage of the portfolio.

                Credit quality, issuer concentration, maturity and liquidity still need to be evaluated carefully. The goal is allocation to diversify around ones' financial needs.

                Bigger Portfolios Need Better Allocation, Not Less Equity

                The current market is a useful illustration of why this distinction matters.

                A roughly 14% decline from the peak can recover. A two-year time correction can eventually end. Long-term investors should not redesign portfolios simply because markets have gone through a difficult period.

                But as the corpus grows, the stakes change. Protecting accumulated wealth becomes as important as pursuing the next leg of growth.

                At ₹10 lakh, the priority may largely be accumulation. At ₹50 lakh, diversification starts to carry more weight. At ₹1 crore and beyond, separating long-term growth capital from money required over the next few years becomes increasingly important.

                The first crore is often built by focusing on returns and compounding.

                Managing the next crore requires something else: making sure each part of the portfolio takes only the risk its time horizon can afford.
